The park offers those traveling to and from either station an ideal location to relax or to recreate in the morning, during a lunch break, or at the end of the day. It also serves as the "front yard" for some of the city's redevelopment efforts, such as the New Jersey Performing Arts Center, the Prudential Tower (completed in 2015), and the recently completed adaptive reuse of the Hahne & Company department store.

In Somerville, upgrades to a connector between the downtown and the Somerville Train Station initially focused on widening sidewalks and other improvements and led to a "shared street" where all users—pedestrians, bicyclists, and drivers—share the road. To facilitate the shared street, designs called for raising the road surface to the sidewalk elevation, which was completed in 2012. Poured concrete used for this project required a two-month curing period, during which time the space was pedestrian-only. This unintentional pilot of a pedestrian-only space struck a chord with residents and visitors, who called for additional consideration of use of the space. A survey conducted in summer 2013 confirmed local preferences and resulted in the state's sole pedestrian-only street. Somerville's Division Street is now an actively programmed space in the heart of the community. Somerville Downtown Alliance, the community's Main Street organization, and Arts on Division, a community-based group promoting art and art education, host frequent events in the space.

One strategy to bring public spaces into a transit-oriented community is to build a park or plaza at (or on top of) a transit facility. The redevelopment of San Francisco's Transbay Center makes such public space a priority. With the completion of its first phase in summer 2018, the new Transbay Center will connect eight Bay Area counties through 11 transportation systems, including AC Transit, BART, Caltrain, Golden Gate Transit, Greyhound, Muni, SamTrans, WestCAT Lynx, Amtrak, Paratransit, and the High Speed Rail Authority, which will eventually connect San Francisco to Los Angeles/Anaheim. Securing the resources to improve, create, or program public space may require creativity, ingenuity, persistence, and, possibly, a bit of luck. New Jersey grant-making organizations with a history of supporting similar projects include the Community Foundation of New Jersey, the Horizon Foundation for New Jersey, and the Victoria Foundation. Still another option may be working with a dedicated private sector partner with a history of philanthropic investment focused on public space, fitness, and/or public health. Such collaborations can be used to fund construction or establish a dedicated management group for the public space.

Ongoing support for public space operations may also come from a variety of sources including grants, event use fees, sponsorship, and contributions from abutting property owners and businesses that benefit from its success. Manage Public Space

A public space management entity is one way to invest in, or revitalize, a public space. Such an entity could be the local parks or recreation department, an existing local non-profit organization, a new non-profit organization dedicated to community public space, or a Business Improvement District (BID). In the wake of suburban developments that are given priority alongside urban planning, there are no single-use downtown neighborhoods anymore. There's a merge of functionalities in each area where residential and commercial developments happen alongside each other. This will thus make way for cities where each area has a mix of functional utilities for housing, work opportunities, and avenues for engagement altogether.
2. Green living
Cities easily lose sight of the connection with nature because of the rapid urbanization they encompass. But to create harmony between people, their lifestyles, and a sense of connection, green corridors are given importance increasingly. Making way for an outdoor engagement activity and green public parks are given added importance these days.

3. The 15-minute city
This refers to the creation of a neighborhood approach where every amenity is available within a 15-minute walking or cycling distance. This will help resolve problems like the need to commute long distances for work, parties, or play. Apart from being just a solution for mobility problems, the 15-minute city also helps in making a city sustainable and self-sufficient in nature. By Frank Edgerton Martin Special to the Star Tribune. November 10, 2017
The words we use to describe cities — such as, "downtown", "central business district" or even "city center" — contain assumptions about what should happen there, who should live there, and how the area should look and feel. We rarely question what we mean when we talk about downtown, especially when it comes to Minneapolis.
It's time to do so.
Our definition of "Downtown" is preventing us from creating a truly urbane, equitable and 24-hour city — a civic landscape where people live, work and play in the central city and surrounding neighborhoods
Loring Park's downtown vista. The Loring neighborhood was filled with pedestrian scale buildings, stores, residential hotels, and churches that flowed into the business and retail core. Linen postcard from the mid-1930s.
In the early 20th century, Minneapolis had a more connected, cohesive feel. You could live in a neighborhood like Stevens Square, which is close to the center of the city, and walk to work downtown.
Along the way, you'd pass from single-family homes to apartment hotels to clusters of small businesses and offices, with the buildings growing larger and more densely spaced the closer to downtown you got.
Historic apartment architecture in Loring Park

Portland, Oregon, for example, is celebrated for reintroducing streetcars downtown. Some planners, looking to invigorate Minneapolis, say Portland should be our model. Downtown is an American term, coined in early 19th century Manhattan. The city started on the island's southern tip. The only direction it could grow was northward (or "up" on maps). "Uptown" (or Upper Manhattan) became a primarily residential area, while downtown was all about commerce, an association that has stuck.
Some cities, including Philadelphia, never adopted the downtown moniker, retaining the more European Center City name for its core. But as newer cities emerged in the west, most embraced the commercial downtown idea, including Minneapolis and St. Paul.

Hybrid work has settled into a durable pattern rather than a temporary disruption, so downtown policy should plan around it instead of waiting for it to reverse.

Industry survey data put the typical hybrid arrangement at two to three office days a week, with US employees returning less than counterparts in Europe or Asia because of longer commutes and larger homes. [shard_05705_47603]

Workplace researchers have found that roughly one and a half to two days of remote work per week is the productivity-optimal, sustainable pattern, even though some executives still expect pressure toward fuller office mandates as firms grow frustrated with hybrid management. [shard_05133_51015]

Real estate analysts similarly expect the office market's "shakeout" to take another four to five years to fully play out, noting that past crises always saw cities rebound but that remote work is a genuinely new variable this time. [shard_04451_72103]

The fiscal backdrop reinforces why waiting is not a viable strategy: major US metro office vacancy reached roughly 53% of pre-pandemic occupancy by January 2024, national office vacancy is near 20% with San Francisco and Los Angeles above 25%, and about $117 billion in office mortgages were due for refinancing in 2024 against buildings running at roughly half their old usage. [shard_06324_66478] [shard_02933_20809] [shard_04660_11309]

Analysts expect this to gradually shift more of the local tax burden onto residential and other commercial property over several years rather than collapsing budgets overnight, which gives a planning committee a window to act deliberately rather than reactively. [shard_06324_66478]

Given that trajectory, the highest-priority lever is converting surplus office stock to housing, but conversions should be pursued selectively rather than as a blanket solution, because only a minority of buildings are physically suited to it. [shard_05928_49470]

Calgary's program, built for buildings with large floor plates and deep vacancy, has produced about 700 new homes from roughly 665,000 square feet of converted office space using per-square-foot subsidies capped at several million dollars per project, while Ottawa paired fee reductions and faster approvals with smaller cash incentives and still saw over 700 conversion units emerge between 2013 and 2022, many without any incentive at all. [shard_01386_41471] [shard_05928_49470]

That pattern suggests committees should target incentives narrowly at genuinely marginal, structurally suitable buildings rather than subsidizing conversions the market would fund anyway, and should expect conversions to add housing and evening population at the margins rather than to solve downtown vacancy on their own.

Transit funding needs the second-highest priority, but the goal should shift from restoring commuter-peak capacity to serving a flatter, more residential ridership pattern. [shard_05777_51189]

Nationally, ridership remains roughly 30% below pre-pandemic levels even years after the initial collapse, and the roughly $70 billion in emergency federal COVID-era transit support that filled agency budgets is expiring, creating a genuine funding cliff rather than a temporary dip. [shard_05777_51189]

Rather than pouring scarce transit dollars into rush-hour-only service built for five-day office commuting, committees should weight investment toward all-day, cross-town, and weekend service that supports a downtown population living, shopping, and socializing there rather than just commuting through it, an approach cities have paired with public-space investment sited at transit hubs and funded partly through incentive zoning that trades developers extra density for parks, plazas, or affordable housing contributions. [shard_01475_4781]

Retail support and public space policy should be treated as the fastest, cheapest wins rather than afterthoughts, since they can respond to today's foot-traffic gap while conversions and transit reform play out over years.

Seattle's Restored program, which gave $2,500 working-capital grants plus marketing and technical support to fill vacant storefronts with pop-ups and arts uses over two-to-four-month terms, and Spokane and Seattle's parallel efforts turning vacant space toward arts, education, and life-sciences uses alongside permanent public-space changes like pedestrianizing part of Pike Place Market and installing a downtown pickleball court, show how modest, flexible programs can restore street-level vitality without waiting for large capital projects. [shard_01495_41805] [shard_01066_64441]

Urban planners increasingly frame the underlying fix as land-use reform rather than incentive layering: the "15-minute city" concept of clustering housing, work, and daily amenities within walking distance, and the related "18-hour city" trend in which downtown residential growth and evening retail and entertainment keep areas active well past a 9-to-5 office cycle, both describe a downtown that generates its own weekday and evening demand instead of depending entirely on commuters. [shard_04005_16689] [shard_01225_12069]

Minneapolis planners have made a related argument that "downtown" itself is a misleading, commerce-only framing inherited from 19th-century zoning, and that a more livable core comes from treating downtown as a connected set of walkable neighborhoods rather than a single business district cut off from surrounding areas by freeways. [shard_05609_62864]

Weighing all of this together, a realistic sequence for the next few years is retail and public-space programs first because they are cheap and immediate, transit service redesign second because funding urgency is high but reform takes budget cycles, targeted office conversions third because they are valuable but structurally limited to a minority of buildings, and mixed-use, neighborhood-style zoning reform as the underlying long-term shift that makes all of the above self-reinforcing rather than dependent on offices refilling to pre-pandemic levels.
